problem_data.story:
The shuttle's engines hummed as it descended through the Martian atmosphere. Lieutenant Samantha Willis checked her weapon one last time before nodding to Captain Raj Bailey.

"Ready when you are, sir."

Bailey straightened his blue helmet—the distinctive mark of the Interplanetary Justice Corps—and reviewed the warrant on his datapad. His jaw was tight in a way Willis hadn't seen before. "Remember, Willis, we're dealing with someone who has spent the last three years building support across the outer colonies. If this goes wrong, we could trigger a secession movement that spans half the solar system."

Willis had seen Bailey handle dozens of missions with cool professionalism. Border disputes between mining claims. Protection details for diplomatic convoys. Even the tense standoff at Ceres Station last year, when armed smugglers had taken hostages. But something about today was different.

"Sir, you seem concerned."

Bailey didn't answer immediately. He was reading something on his datapad—legal precedents, it looked like. "The IJC has been around since 2087. We've enforced the Mars Settlement Accords, handled everything from resource disputes to weapons violations. But there are limits to what we've actually tested in practice."

The shuttle banked hard, and Willis grabbed a handhold. Through the viewport, she could see the rust-colored Martian landscape spreading toward the horizon.

"Limits, sir?"

"The Accords give us broad authority. On paper, we can enforce laws against anyone who violates the terms. But paper authority and practical authority aren't the same thing." He set down the datapad. "When was the last time we actually moved against someone with real political power? Someone who could rally half the solar system to their cause?"

Willis thought about it. Most of their targets were criminals—smugglers, illegal weapons dealers, rogue mining operations. People without constituencies. People whose arrest wouldn't make headlines beyond the local news feeds.

"I can't think of one," she admitted.

"Neither can I. And that's what worries me."

Willis had grown up in the lower districts of Newbridge Town, Earth's largest arcology. Her father had worked in recycling management, sorting waste for fourteen hours a day. Her mother had been a data entry clerk for a logistics company. Neither had ever left Earth's surface.

"You could get a good job right here," her mother had said when Samantha announced her enlistment. "The arcologies always need security personnel. You could live two levels up from us. Maybe three, with your test scores."

"I don't want to live in Newbridge my whole life," Samantha had replied.

"What's wrong with Newbridge? We gave you everything. Your father worked himself to exhaustion so you could have a good education."

"I want to do something that matters."

Her father had looked up from his entertainment feed. "The IJC? You know they're basically the enforcement arm of Earth's colonial policy. You'll spend your life making sure Mars and the Belt stay under Earth's thumb."

"That's not what they do. They keep the peace. They prevent wars."

"By threatening anyone who steps out of line."

She had left anyway. Six months of training on Luna, learning zero-G combat, studying interplanetary law, mastering the use of non-lethal weapons systems. The instructors had been hard but fair. She'd learned that the Corps recruited two types: idealists who believed in preventing interplanetary conflict, and opportunists who wanted adventure and prestige.

Samantha wasn't sure which category she fell into.

The shuttle touched down at Camden Spaceport in Estoria, Mars's third-largest city. From the landing pad, Willis could see a gleaming dome that housed the regional government—administrative offices, meeting halls, and reception spaces for official functions.

"We go in quiet," Bailey said. "No weapons visible unless necessary. There's a reception happening for the Asteroid Mining Consortium. Lots of witnesses, which is good for us."

They passed through security using their IJC credentials. The guards looked nervous but didn't interfere. Everyone knew what the blue helmets meant.

The reception hall was full of wealthy miners and colonial administrators. Their target stood at the center, a tall man with silver hair and an easy smile. He was discussing cultural anthropology with a professor from the University of Mars—something about how isolated colonial communities developed distinct value systems.

Bailey approached with Willis two steps behind. "Governor Chen, I'm Captain Raj Bailey of the Interplanetary Justice Corps. This is Lieutenant Willis. We have a warrant for your arrest."

The room went silent.

Chen took the datapad and read carefully. When he finished, he smiled—the practiced smile of a politician who had faced down challenges before. "An interesting legal argument, Captain. But I think you'll find this matter isn't quite so simple."

"The warrant is valid, sir."

"Valid according to whom? The Accords were written to handle disputes between mining operations and to prevent arms buildups. They weren't designed to let Earth reach into colonial governments and extract elected officials." Chen gestured at the assembled crowd. "These people elected me. Three times. Do you think they'll accept having their democratic choice overruled by officers who answer to Earth?"

A murmur ran through the room. Willis noticed several of the guests moving closer, their expressions hostile.

"The law applies to everyone," Bailey said.

"Laws require consent to function, Captain. And you're about to discover how little consent you actually have." Chen turned as if to walk away, then paused. "I've spent my career trying to build something here. Cultural institutions. Economic independence. A future where Mars isn't just Earth's mining colony. If you arrest me, you won't be enforcing the law. You'll be proving that Earth sees us as subjects, not partners."

Bailey's hand moved to his weapon. "If you attempt to leave, sir, I'll be forced to restrain you."

"You wouldn't dare. Do you know what would happen? Every colony from here to Titan would demand independence. You need me in court, Captain, not dead. And I don't think your young lieutenant there has the nerve to actually shoot me."

Willis felt her hand move to her weapon. Bailey's hand came up in a subtle stop gesture.

"Lieutenant Willis may be young," Bailey said, "but she's an expert marksman. And she understands what's at stake here."

Chen studied them both for a long moment. Then he straightened his jacket and addressed the crowd. "Ladies and gentlemen, you're witnessing the true face of Earth's authority. Officers with guns, arresting your elected representative for the crime of building a future for Mars."

He turned to walk toward the exit. Bailey moved with practiced precision, striking Chen at the base of the neck with a nerve disruptor. The governor collapsed.

"Help! They're kidnapping the governor!"

Bailey pulled a gas capsule from his belt and dropped it. Purple stun mist filled the immediate area. Two security guards rushed in and collapsed, their nervous systems temporarily paralyzed.

"Get him to the shuttle," Bailey ordered.

Willis helped drag Chen's unconscious form toward the exit. Behind them, she heard shouting and the sound of weapons being drawn. Bailey threw another capsule, and more guards fell twitching to the floor.

Their shuttle pilot, Youssef Grant, had the engines running. "How'd it go?"

"They'll be mobilizing the Colonial Guard in about thirty seconds," Bailey said.

Grant swore. "The spaceport's going to be locked down before we can launch."

"Then we use the backup plan. Willis, you remember the coordinates?"

She nodded. There was a climate research station in Rosewood Province, about two hundred kilometers south. The station had a matter transmitter—one of the few on Mars that could send directly to Earth. The transmitter network had revolutionized interplanetary travel, but the technology was still expensive. Most colonies only had a handful of stations.

"They'll figure out where we're going," Willis said.

"That's why we have to get there first."

The shuttle lifted off as security vehicles converged on the spaceport. Grant pushed the engines to maximum, skimming low over the Martian surface. Behind them, three Colonial Guard interceptors gave chase.

Willis had never been in combat before. She'd trained for it, run simulations, but this was different. Real weapons. Real danger.

"Incoming fire!" Grant shouted.

The shuttle rocked as an energy bolt struck the rear shields. Warning lights flashed across the control panel.

"Can we make it?" Bailey asked.

"If they don't hit us again."

Through the viewport, Willis could see the rust-colored landscape rushing past. Mars had always seemed romantic in the vids—humanity's first true colony world, the frontier of civilization. Now it just looked empty and hostile.

Another bolt struck them. The shuttle lurched sideways.

"Shields at forty percent," Grant reported.

"How much farther?"

"Five minutes. Maybe less if I can coax more speed out of these engines."

Bailey turned to Willis. "When we land, we're going to have to move fast. The research station only has a skeleton crew. We'll secure the transmitter, send Chen through to Earth, then follow."

"What if the Colonial Guard gets there first?"

"Then we fight our way out."

Willis checked her weapon again. The standard IJC sidearm fired various non-lethal rounds—stun charges, neural disruptors, adhesive foam. But she also had a locker in the back with lethal options. Just in case.

"There's the station," Grant said.

The climate research facility was a cluster of prefab domes connected by pressurized tunnels. It sat on the edge of a massive canyon, surrounded by wind turbines and solar arrays. Scientists came here to study Martian weather patterns and test new atmospheric processors.

Grant brought the shuttle down hard, scraping the landing gear against rock. "Go! I'll try to hold off the Guard."

Bailey and Willis dragged Chen's unconscious body out of the shuttle. The Martian gravity made him easier to carry than he would have been on Earth, but the thin atmosphere meant they needed respirators.

They burst into the main dome. A scientist in a lab coat looked up in surprise.

"IJC business," Bailey said. "We need to use your transmitter."

"I... you can't just—"

"Where is it?"

The scientist pointed to a door marked "Transmission Facility."

Behind them, they heard the roar of the Colonial Guard interceptors landing. Bailey swore and pulled out his weapon. "Willis, get Chen to the transmitter. I'll hold them here."

"Sir, you can't—"

"That's an order, Lieutenant."

Willis hesitated for just a moment, then dragged Chen toward the transmission facility. Behind her, she heard Bailey shouting for the scientists to evacuate, then the distinctive whine of stun weapons firing.

The transmission chamber was a circular room with a raised platform in the center. Control panels lined the walls. Willis had been trained in basic transmitter operation, but she'd never actually used one.

She laid Chen on the platform and rushed to the controls. Destination: Geneva, Earth. The IJC headquarters. She entered her authorization codes and initiated the sequence.

The door burst open. Colonial Guard soldiers poured in, weapons raised.

"Step away from the controls!"

Willis drew her sidearm. "I'm an IJC officer executing a lawful warrant. Stand down."

"You're kidnapping our governor!"

The transmitter hummed as it powered up. Thirty seconds until transmission.

"Last warning," the lead soldier said. "Step away or we fire."

Willis thought about her father, watching entertainment feeds in their small apartment. She thought about Bailey, holding off an entire squad to buy her time. She thought about Chen's words in the reception hall—about democracy and consent and what it meant to enforce laws on people who didn't recognize your authority.

She fired a stun charge at the lead soldier. He dropped. The others returned fire.

Pain exploded in her shoulder as an energy bolt caught her. She fell against the control panel, fighting to stay conscious. Another bolt hit her leg.

The transmitter activated. Chen's body vanished in a flash of light.

Willis collapsed to the floor. The soldiers surrounded her, weapons pointed at her head.

"Is he gone?" one of them asked.

"Yeah. Transmitted to Earth."

"Damn it. Secure the prisoner."

Through the haze of pain, Willis heard one of them calling for a medic. She'd done it. Chen was in custody. The mission was complete.

But she'd never felt so alone.

---

Six weeks later, after she'd recovered enough to travel, Willis returned to Earth. The trial had been a media sensation. Chen's defense attorneys had argued that the IJC had overstepped its bounds, that the Accords had never been intended to give Earth authority over elected colonial leaders.

The prosecution had presented evidence of secret military buildups—weapons stockpiles, training facilities, encrypted communications with sympathetic administrators across the outer colonies. Chen had been preparing for something, though his defenders claimed it was purely defensive, a response to Earth's increasingly aggressive posture.

In the end, the tribunal convicted him of violating the Mars Settlement Accords—specifically, the provisions limiting colonial military forces. Whether the conviction would hold up to appeals, and whether the colonies would accept the verdict, remained to be seen.

Captain Bailey had died holding off the Colonial Guard. He'd taken down fifteen soldiers before they'd overwhelmed him. The IJC posthumously promoted him to Major and named a new training facility on Luna after him.

Willis received the Solar Cross, the highest decoration the Corps could award. Her mother kept it in a display case in their apartment, next to her father's employee service awards.

"I still don't understand why you did it," her father said when she visited. "Bailey was your superior officer. You could have surrendered. You didn't have to risk your life."

Samantha looked at the medal. She thought about Bailey's lectures on justice theory and moral philosophy, about how the law meant nothing if no one was willing to enforce it. She thought about Grant, who'd been captured but survived. She thought about the scientists at the research station who'd been caught in the crossfire.

"Someone had to do it," she said finally. "If we'd let Chen go, every colony in the solar system would have known they could ignore Earth's authority. There would have been chaos."

"But why did it have to be you?"

She didn't have a good answer. She'd made a choice in that moment, standing in the transmission facility with weapons pointed at her. She'd decided that something was more important than her own survival.

The psychologists had been surprised. Her enlistment profile had suggested she was motivated primarily by career advancement and desire for status. Nothing indicated she would sacrifice herself for an abstract principle.

But people were more complicated than profiles suggested.

"I'm going back," she told her parents. "They've offered me a promotion. Captain. My own team."

Her mother looked worried. Her father just shook his head.

"You really want to do this for the rest of your life? Risking everything for people who don't even appreciate it?"

Samantha looked out the window at the arcology's lower levels, where her parents had spent their entire lives. Where she would have spent hers, if she hadn't left.

"Yeah," she said. "I do."

She reported to IJC headquarters the next morning. They gave her a new team, a new mission. There were always disputes to settle, laws to enforce, people who thought they could ignore the rules that kept civilization from tearing itself apart.

Someone had to do it.

And Samantha Willis had discovered she was willing to be that someone.

Her first mission as captain took her to Glendale, Ulvaria—a mining colony on one of Jupiter's moons where the local administrator was accused of exploiting workers. A routine case, by IJC standards. Nothing like what they'd faced on Mars.

But that was a problem for tomorrow.

Today, she put on her blue helmet and reported for duty.

The helmet felt heavier than she remembered. Or maybe she just understood better what it meant to wear it.

Either way, she wore it with pride.
